title: Mastering Pediatric Disc Edema: Papilledema vs. Pseudopapilledema
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to the evaluation of pediatric optic disc swelling. This poster highlights the critical differentiation between true intracranial pressure-related papilledema and masqueraders like optic disc drusen.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Mechanism
sections.content: Papilledema is optic disc swelling secondary to raised intracranial pressure (ICP). It is almost always bilateral. Pathophysiology: Axoplasmic flow stasis at the lamina cribrosa due to increased CSF pressure in the subarachnoid space surrounding the optic nerve. In a 12-year-old, this necessitates rapid exclusion of intracranial mass, hydrocephalus, or idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH).

rows: Bilateral, venous tortuosity, flame hemorrhages, obscured margins
Unilateral, pain with eye movement, RAPD, central scotoma
Altitudinal field loss, disc pallor, older age
Blood and thunder fundus, intraretinal hemorrhages
Anomalous discs, absent spontaneous venous pulsations (SVP) not always reliable

sections.title: Red Flags for Pediatric Disc Edema
content: Presence of sixth nerve (abducens) palsy (lateral rectus weakness)
Neurological focal deficits or altered mental status
Failure to thrive or growth disturbances (suggesting hypothalamic involvement)

branches: True Papilledema: Hyperemia, obscured vessels, SVP absent
Disc Drusen: Buried early, visible calcification later, SVP present, crisp margins
Hyperopia/Crowded Discs: Small disc size, normal retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Complete ophthalmic exam (BCVA, Color vision, Pupils for RAPD).
Step 2: Fundus Photography and OCT of the RNFL (look for thickening).
Step 3: B-Scan Ultrasound (detecting high reflectivity of drusen).
Step 4: Neuroimaging (MRI Brain + Orbit with/without contrast + MRV).
Step 5: Lumbar Puncture (if MRI is negative to measure opening pressure).

sections.title: Long-term Sequelae of Optic Disc Drusen
content: Progressive calcification and enlargement of drusen
Non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) risk
Visual field constriction (nasal steps or arcuate defects)
Gradual retinal nerve fiber layer thinning

content.explanation: Vascular, Infection, Neoplasm, Degenerative, Iatrogenic/Intracranial, Congenital, Autoimmune, Trauma, Endocrine.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Spontaneous Venous Pulsation (SVP): Its presence strongly suggests normal intracranial pressure.
OCT RNFL values: >120 microns usually indicates pathological swelling.
Optic Disc Drusen: Highly reflective on ultrasound; look for a 'shadowing' effect.
IIH Management: In pediatric populations, weight management and acetazolamide are first-line.
